summary:
Çankırı province stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBT people has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison, and would allow charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 under civil-code article 40 and condition that care on permanent infertility, with providers exposed to fines and up to seven years and patients up to three. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch called for withdrawal. The measure had not been enacted when reported, and its pending status has not prevented authorities elsewhere in Turkey from applying the prohibitions in practice: in 2025 Istanbul police stopped around 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district and held them for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release, with foreign visitors required to produce original identity documents at such stops.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published 24 February 2026, documents 313 right-to-liberty violations in the year, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total and mostly detentions, alongside 299 detention decisions, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations up from 51, and six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected. The organisation attributes the shift to "Year of the Family" instructions from senior officials directed at public institutions.

Turkey keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the documentary base relies on media coverage and rights-group monitoring. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, which makes every checkpoint interaction an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Neither source identifies a specific incident, enforcement action or prosecution in Çankırı. The national figures reflect where monitoring is concentrated rather than a measured difference between provinces, and the absence of a recorded event in Çankırı should not be read as an assessment that conditions there are more permissive.
tangentialFactors:
Documented enforcement is concentrated in the country's largest city, where 2025 street stops of trans women for background checks produced no fines but generated records of each woman stopped. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue the checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

The pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

The asymmetry of state response is a further marker. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and in August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker who was released while the victim was referred for arrest.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the risk of the draft 11th Judicial Package becoming law, including the rise in the age of gender-affirming care to 25 with a permanent-infertility requirement and criminal exposure for providers and patients alike. Transition-related care is already tightening through regulation: a Health Ministry measure reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records.

Custody conditions follow registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; branches of the Human Rights Association in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison.

The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted remains unresolved at the source dates; Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and does not record its passage.

No province-specific enforcement, incident, prosecution or police practice in Çankırı is documented in either source, and both are national in scope. Whether the pattern of street stops and background checks observed in the country's largest city occurs in Çankırı is not sourced either way.

Local service availability is unresolved: no source addresses whether LGBT organisations, trans-specific shelter, competent healthcare providers or gender-marker services operate in Çankırı, and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation's application in provincial hospitals is not sourced.

The documentary base itself is limited by the state's absence of official hate-crime statistics, so Kaos GL's figures rest on media monitoring; incidents that go unreported cannot be ruled out.
